idiom_name: nominal type + private construction + one immutable instance per constant + boundary converters
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare one nominal type that owns the closed set, make construction private (or make the declared members the only inhabitants of the type), and export exactly one immutable instance per alternative. Put the name, the external value and any behaviour on the member itself, and keep a single pair of conversion functions (format/parse) for representations from outside, validating unknown values there. Raw primitives must never flow into the domain type without that conversion, and any member set that crosses persistence, wire or ABI boundaries needs explicitly assigned external values.
code_sketch:
type Suit = Clubs | Diamonds | Hearts | Spades   # nominal, closed set
suit: Suit = Clubs                           # only members type-check
parse(text): Suit | error                    # validate once, at the boundary
members(Suit) -> [Clubs, Diamonds, Hearts, Spades]
pitfalls: Allowing implicit conversion from the underlying primitive defeats the pattern: the type is then only a prettier int or string.
Persisting ordinals or implicit values couples stored data to declaration order.
Adding a member breaks every exhaustive match; plan for the switch sites or delegate behaviour to the members.

Wrong move: subclassing the underlying primitive (Python IntEnum/StrEnum, TypeScript numeric enums) because a comparison wanted a raw int or string -> every int or number then satisfies the type again and arithmetic leaks back into the domain, which is why the Python docs restrict IntEnum/StrEnum to interoperability only -> keep the members nominal and convert to the primitive inside the boundary converter.

Wrong move: indexing arrays by ordinal()/values()[i] or trusting values().length to size enum-keyed storage -> inserting or reordering a member silently shifts every stored position (generated Java enums even hit bytecode limits around 1,700 values, so the member count is a real capacity constraint) -> assign explicit stable tags and look members up by tag, never by position.

Wrong move: publishing ambient const enums in .d.ts files because inlining removes indirection -> consumers inline version A's values while running version B, taking wrong branches that same-version CI never catches -> avoid exporting const enums, or emit them with preserveConstEnums so consumers bind at runtime.
